hints: Focus on what thermal cracking really does, it breaks long carbon chains into smaller fragments by breaking C-C bonds.
Notice oct-1-ene is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}$, so any pair of fragments you make must add back to 8 carbons and 16 hydrogens in total.
Try pairing each of W, X, Y and Z with a suitable partner fragment to balance C and H, remembering alkanes, alkenes and dienes are all allowed.
walkthrough:
**Recall what thermal cracking allows**

Cracking breaks a C-C single bond in a long chain to give two smaller molecules. For an alkene starting material, the products can be alkenes, alkanes and even dienes, as long as atoms balance.

Starting molecule:
$$\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 = \text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}$$

**Check ethene W and propene X**

These are classic short alkenes from cracking. For example, breaking off a 2-carbon or 3-carbon end leaves a longer alkene.
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12} + \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$$
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_{10} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2$$

**Check propane Y and butadiene Z**

Many students think only alkenes form, but H atoms can redistribute. An alkane fragment can form if the other fragment gains an extra double bond to balance H.
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_8 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + \text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}=\text{CH}_2$$

**Conclude the combination**

Since balanced equations can be written for W, X, Y and Z, all four can be obtained from different cracking pathways of oct-1-ene.

options.A: Correct. Ethene and propene form with a longer alkene partner, while propane forms with a diene partner ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$) and butadiene forms with an alkane partner ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$). All balance to $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}$, so W, X, Y and Z are all possible.
options.B: Incorrect. This correctly includes W, X and Y but wrongly leaves out butadiene Z. Students choose this thinking dienes cannot form in cracking, but a diene plus an alkane balances perfectly.
options.C: Incorrect. This correctly includes W, X and Z but wrongly leaves out propane Y. Students choose this thinking alkanes cannot come from cracking an alkene, but they can when the co-product is a diene with two double bonds.
options.D: Incorrect. This includes only the two simple alkenes W and X. It is the trap for thinking cracking of an alkene gives only alkenes, forgetting that alkane plus diene combinations also conserve C and H.
